en: Homage to the illustrious Bhūtaḍāmara!
By whom bodies, families, goddesses, and family leaders were created for the sake of the welfare of the world—
he, whose single reality follows the mudrās of those forms.
Let that Vajradhara be sought for the sake of auspiciousness.
In this world, few have mastered the *Mahāmāyātantra*, which is exceedingly light in its words yet profound in its meaning;
therefore, for those who possess pure learning, knowledge of it exists at every step.
This is my effort to make [it] easily attainable in this world in a discreet manner.
The Sugata has taught various paths to enlightenment, having observed that the world has diverse inclinations;
many have set out on their own according to their own preferences.
My commentary here is indeed possessed of merit; now, as for the action [to be performed]...

"Then," and so forth. This tantra is not independent (*muktaka*). What then? It is a composite (*saṃyuktaka*) joined with other tantras. Therefore, this word "then" (*atha*) indicates the immediate succession of this tantra in relation to a preceding tantra. For this very reason, the introductory formula of the "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth is not employed at the beginning of this work, because it has already been employed previously. As in the *Śrīvajraśikhara*: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) means because this alone is the swift means for attaining awakening for those who delight in extreme brevity; therefore, the connection is "I shall proclaim. "I shall proclaim" (*pravakṣye*) means I shall speak after having analyzed [the subject].
"Tantra" means a continuous composition (*prabandha*).
Tantra is threefold: causal tantra (*hetu-tantra*), resultant tantra (*phala-tantra*), and method tantra (*upāya-tantra*).
Among these, the mind that is naturally luminous and without beginning or end is the *bodhicitta*. That is the cause; it is the seed. Of what is it the seed? Of awakening (*bodhi*).

Perfectly complete enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is the fruit, because it is the unsurpassed fruit. Furthermore, that is the purification characterized by the exhaustion of all adventitious obscurations of that very mind which is luminous by nature. That is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas; the meaning is that it is the basis for the infinite Buddha-qualities comprised within the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. That itself is the awakening of the Buddhas, the *dharmakāya*, the state of the Great Vajra-holder.

Therefore, the means (*upāya*) is the practice for the complete accomplishment of that fruit. Furthermore, for Bodhisattvas, this is the path together with its auxiliary factors, cultivated over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

In the Mantra Vehicle (*mantrayāna*), however, it is the means—the path together with its auxiliary factors—consisting of the forms of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, which is a condensed form of that very same vast path to enlightenment, and which accomplishes enlightenment more swiftly and more easily.

With reference to these causes, fruits, and means, those continuous teachings are, respectively, the Causal Tantra (*hetutantra*), the Fruitional Tantra (*phalatantra*), and the Means Tantra (*upāyatantra*). I shall explain this threefold tantra.

Now, as to what the name of that tantra is, he says: "It is named the Supreme Secret. The word *nāma* is an indeclinable used in the sense of being well-known; the meaning is that it is renowned by the name "Supreme Secret.
To whom is it the supreme secret? He says: "Of the Vajra-Ḍākinīs."

Therefore, this tantra is named *Vajraḍākinī-paramaguhyam* in its entirety; however, by eliding the first member of the compound, it is called *Paramaguhyam*, just as *Satyabhāmā* is called *Bhāmā*. The root *ḍai* means "to move through the air. The vowel *ai* becomes *ā*. The act of flying (*ḍānam*) is *ḍāḥ*; the meaning is "moving through space. From the word *ḍā*, the third case suffix is applied: *ak*, *ag*. The root *kuṭ* means "to go crookedly. Here, moving everywhere is the "crooked motion. She whose nature (*śīlam*) it is to fly (*akitum*) is a *ḍākinī*. The meaning is that she moves simultaneously in all directions by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodies. And so it has been said:
The verbal root *ḍai* is here interpreted as "moving through the air";
thus, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of moving everywhere in space is called *ḍākinī*, according to the etymological derivation.
The mention of "vajra" is for the purpose of excluding external ḍākinīs;

they are "vajras" because they consist of non-conceptual wisdom (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*). And they are "ḍākinīs"; thus, they are "Vajra-ḍākinīs. To the question of what kind of beings they are, he says: "of the mistresses of the secret" (*guhyeśvarīṇām*). Here, there are five families (*kula*) and five secrets. Their mistresses are those who effect emanation and reabsorption. Among them, [the first] is the mistress of the Tathāgata family.

The Buddha-Ḍākinī; the Vajra-Ḍākinī of the Vajra family; the Ratna-Ḍākinī of the Maṇi family; the Padma-Ḍākinī of the Padma family; and Viśva-Ḍākinī, the sovereign of the Karma family. Even their sovereign is Mahāmāyā.
Because she is the secret among those secrets that are exceedingly secret, she is the "Supreme Secret" (paramaguhyam).
The tantra that expresses her is also called by that same name, just as the poem [entitled] *Sītāharaṇa* is so named. || 3 ||

To demonstrate the meaning of this very name, he says "yayā" and so forth. [The root] *bṛh* or *bṛhi* means "to grow. With the suffix *manin*, and with a phonetic alteration (*varṇavikāra*) according to etymological rules (*nairukta*), it becomes *brahma*. Here, however, because they are the gurus of all worlds and have grown in every respect, the *brahmāṇas* are the Tathāgatas comprised within the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) and emanation (*nirmāṇa*) bodies. Their *aṇḍa* is the place of origin; the meaning is the *dharmakāya*. Alternatively, because it is the excellence of liberation (*mokṣa*), it is *brahma*; and because it is the place of origin for those two bodies, it is an *aṇḍa*; thus, *brahmāṇḍa* means the *dharmakāya*.

In the completely pure Buddha-fields, that which is the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) is the "moving" (*cara*) here; that which is the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*) therein is the "non-moving" (*acara*) here. That which exists together with those two is the "moving and non-moving" (*sacarācara*) universe (*brahmāṇḍa*). The grammatical connection is that [the reality] pervades that [universe]. "Entire" (*sakala*) means "all"; the meaning is "belonging to all the Tathāgatas. In that regard, how is the universe pervaded by her? Because the universe of all Buddhas is composed of nothing but that. Why are the moving and non-moving worlds pervaded by her? Because they arise from her.

He says this very thing with the words beginning "origination" (*utpatti*). "Origination" means the cause. "Of all the gods" refers to the five *kula*-ḍākinīs. "Brahmā and the others" refers to the five Tathāgatas and their respective lineages, each of which is infinite.
"Possessing great supernatural power" (*maharddhika*) means having great majesty. (4)
He said, "What is *kāsāva*? [The answer is: "It is *mahāmāyā*. By the term *mahāmāyā*, the Lord Heruka—the most secret form of the Blessed One Vajradhara—is expressed.

Regarding "the Great Mistress" (*maheśvarī*): for Brahmā and the others are the creators of the goddesses, and thus they are their lords (*īśvara*). Since they too are created by her, she is the Great Mistress (*maheśvarī*). Because she is the Great Mistress, she is therefore the supreme secret of them. "Of them" means of the Vajra-Ḍākinīs. "Supreme secret" means the highest secret. "This" refers to Mahāmāyā.

For it is thus: subtle form is said to be the secret of gross forms. Consequently, the five lords of the families are the five secrets of the five families, because the five families consist of those [secrets]. Furthermore, the five ḍākinīs are the secrets even of the secrets; for the Lords of the Families have the characteristic of being luminosity that pervades their own respective families, and by virtue of that, they are gross, because they prioritize the aspect of existence (*bhāva*). The ḍākinīs, however, have the characteristic of the emptiness of duality within that very luminosity; therefore, they are subtle, because they prioritize the aspect of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Among those [mantras] which are secret beyond the secret, Mahāmāyā is the secret. For they are coarse because they each possess the specific characteristic of the nature (*dharmatā*) of a single family; this, however, is the common nature of the five families, being the equality of all five of them. Therefore, since she is the secret even of those, she is the supreme secret. Because it expresses that, this tantra is also called the supreme secret. [The question is asked: "Let the supreme secret be explained; but how is Mahāmāyā so called? To this he says: "Mahāmāyā," and so forth.

She is indeed "Greatly Fierce" (*mahāraudrā*) because she is supremely destructive. Why? Because she effects the destruction of the *bhūtas*. Since everything that arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) is an obscuration to the awakening of a Buddha, she is the one who effects its destruction—that is, the agent of its dissolution (*pralaya*). For that dissolution is the supreme liberation.

She is thought of thus: she is *māyā* because she measures (*mināti*). The root *mīñ* means "to injure"; there is the substitution of *ā* (the *ātva* change), and the suffix *ṇa*. Thus ends [verse] 5.

He states another method with the words beginning "by which" (*yayā*), and so forth. "The three worlds" (*trailokya*) refers to the completely pure Buddha-field. "With all that moves and is stationary" (*sacarācara*) is as explained before. It is "pervaded" because [the field] has arisen from that; for she is indeed the *dharmakāya*, and this world of moving and stationary things is its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). He thinks thus: "She creates" (*nirmimīte*) means "illusion" (*māyā*); the root *māṅ* means "to measure," and the suffix *-ṇa* is applied.

He states another method as well, beginning with "She, moreover," and so forth. "Moreover" (punar) means furthermore; that is, another method. "She, this very one" refers to Mahāmāyā in the form of Heruka. "She withdraws the three worlds" because she reduces Maheśvara and other wicked beings to ashes by a mere glance. "Then afterwards she emits [them]" because, having purified them of their faults, she restores them to life by the sounds of the great banners and bells. 6.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the Guhyakas," and so forth. The deities of the external Vajra family are called *guhyaka*s because they are slightly secret (*īṣad-guhyatvāt*). She is their mother; the meaning is "she who gives birth" (*mātrī*). Therefore, she is renowned and celebrated as *Mahāmāyā*. The sense is that the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the roots *mīñ* and *māṅ*, as previously explained.

Let it be that she herself is thus; however, what does she do for practitioners? To this he says: "The three worlds," and so forth. Because her intrinsic nature is unsurpassed gnosis (*jñāna*), she is a *vidyā*. This *vidyā* named Mahāmāyā accomplishes the three worlds for practitioners. "All desires" refers to all intentions, such as the state of a *vidyādhara* and so on; she bestows these preeminently. This half-verse is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) begins with "by which... and extends up to "by means of this yoga-māyā-vidyā. (7)

"By which vidyā"—meaning by that which is the sovereign (*īśvarī*) of practitioners (*sādhaka*). "Merely upon being known"—meaning merely upon being performed. The connection is: "they succeed among the practitioners. To the question "Who succeeds?", he says: "The gods," and so forth. The gods are Śakra and others; the *dānavas* are those with great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), such as pretas; the *gandharvas* are Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others. They are so called because they exist together with the *yakṣas* and so on. "Among the practitioners" means of the practitioners. "They succeed" means they become subject to one's will. (8–9)
"Subjection" (*vaśam*) means being brought under control.

"Beings" (*bhūtāni*) refers to sentient creatures. "Aquatic" refers to crocodiles and the like; "terrestrial" refers to tigers and the like. Thus far, it has been indicated that she is the means for accomplishing the external triple world.
Now, in order to indicate that she is also the means for accomplishing the supramundane triple world, he says: "Prakṛti," and so forth.

Here, the causal tantra (*hetutantra*) is taught in brief by means of half a verse; the resultant tantra (*phalatantra*) is indicated by the line of the verse beginning with "of the self-arisen ones possessing the five gnoses" (*svayambhūpañcajñāninām*); and the method tantra (*upāyatantra*) is taught by the third, fifth, and sixth lines. "Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to one's own innate disposition (*nijaḥ svabhāvaḥ*). By that [nature], they are "luminous" (*prabhāsvara*), meaning they have the quality of shining forth; the sense is that they are exceedingly stainless. Who, then, are they? He says: "phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*). Because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), "phenomena" refers to all things.

Furthermore, all those objects are mind-only, because it is the mind itself that appears in various forms. For example, in a dream, [things appear] in the form of houses, gardens, ponds, elephants, horses, humans, and so forth; and since mental factors (*caitasika*) are also particular states of the mind, [they too are mind-only].
And it is said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"This is mind-only; that is to say, the triple world.
It is also stated in the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra*:
"External objects do not exist in the way they are conceptualized by the foolish."
"The mind, stirred by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), arises as the appearance of objects.
"Stirred by latent impressions" means afflicted or corrupted by latent impressions.

"May all phenomena be mind-only; however, from what [source] are they naturally luminous and radiant? To this he says: "From the beginning," and so forth. "Ā" refers to the beginning of the beginning (*āder ādiḥ*). The meaning is "from the very outset. They are pure because of the absence of all stains of obscuration. They are untroubled because of the absence of the latencies of defilement. The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); because they are pure from the beginning, therefore they are naturally luminous. Because they are naturally luminous, therefore they are radiant by nature.

[Objection: But if impurities (*mala*) and their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) exist, how can [beings] be pure and unsullied? [Response: Because those impurities, which do not possess that [pure] nature, are adventitious (*āgantuka*) to it—just as darkness, frost, smoke, clouds, and dust are to space. Therefore, they are luminous by nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). If this were not so, then no one would attain awakening (*bodhi*); for since impurities are of the very nature of the mind, they could not be destroyed as long as the mind exists. Therefore, the luminosity of the nature of the mind is the cause of awakening, and awakening is the result.

Furthermore, that awakening is the ultimate purification of the mental continuum through the exhaustion of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies. That itself is the *dharmakāya*, because it is the body, the abode, and the support for those phenomena comprised within the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. (10)

In that regard, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are self-arisen (*svayaṃbhū*) by virtue of the Dharma-body; they exist as such through their own nature alone, due to the exhaustion of all obscurations and the state of absolute uniqueness (*kaivalya*). Because they manifest in their very own form, they possess five cognitions (*pañcajñāna*) by means of the three bodies. Their five cognitions are: the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*), the cognition of equality (*samatājñāna*), the cognition of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the cognition of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), and the cognition of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).

Therein, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is as stainless as a polished mirror, infinite and eternal; it is the support for the three intermediate types of wisdom. It is the locus where the reflections of all other forms of wisdom arise. Through the arising of these reflections, the Tathāgatas become perceivers of all phenomena in all their aspects.

The wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is the knowledge that one's own self is no different from all sentient beings; it is always conjoined with great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*). The wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge, a treasury of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), a manifestor of all its own majestic powers within the circles of assemblies, and a showerer of the great rains of Dharma.

That gnosis by which Tathāgatas, through infinite emanations of body, speech, and mind in all world-realms, accomplish the welfare of infinite sentient beings at every moment—that is their gnosis of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

That gnosis by which the Tathāgatas perceive the perfectly pure suchness of all phenomena arises from seeing that alone, because all stains of signs are absolutely non-apparent. This is their gnosis of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

The first three gnoses constitute the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the fourth is the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and the fifth is a portion of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). And they are self-arisen (*svayaṃbhū*).
And because they possess the five knowledges, they are so described; that is to say, they are Tathāgatas.
The means (*upāya*) that result in those fruits are proclaimed and taught primarily therein. "Therein" means while that cause—namely, the intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*)—exists.

For this fruit does not arise even when the cause is present without the means; otherwise, because the cause is beginningless, it would follow that everyone would attain awakening from the very outset. Therefore, the means are proclaimed.

To the question "Who are they?", he says: "The Yoginīs," and so forth. "Yoginīs" refers to the five Ḍākinīs. "Yogamātā" refers to Mahāmāyā. "The three realms without exception" means the entire triple world; from these very [deities] the Lords of the Families and the Families themselves have arisen.

How are these [the three secrets] contained within the triple world? Because they are included within the three vajra-realms, which are the secrets of the Tathāgatas. How are these the skillful means (*upāya*)? Because when the perfection of the cause—which is characterized by the fitness for enlightenment—exists, one swiftly attains enlightenment through the cultivation of these very [secrets] along with their accessories such as recitation (*jāpa*). And once that [enlightenment] has been attained, one causes others to attain the three types of enlightenment according to their respective capacities, by means of these very [secrets] as comprised within the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). || 11 ||

"It is accomplished" means that it is perfected for practitioners both in the form of the path and in the form of the fruit. "By the mere knowledge of which" refers to this very triad of the *yoginī*s and so forth. "Without remainder and without exception" means: without exception because not even a single member of the triad is abandoned; without remainder because not even a single deity is abandoned. It is both without remainder and without exception. Why is it accomplished? Because everything is a magical emanation (*māyā-vikurvita*); the meaning is that all of this, in the states of both the path and the fruit, is dependent upon the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*).
That which was previously indicated as "the accomplisher of the three worlds" has now been explained.

Now he speaks in order to explain that which was indicated as "the bestower of all desires," beginning with the words "she takes away," and so forth. She "takes away" means she draws [them] in, whether for her own sake or for the sake of others. "Of the Buddhas" means the Buddhas. "She enjoys" means, having drawn them in, she makes use of them. "The foremost of gods" means the best of gods, such as Śakra and others. || 12 ||

Yogas are meditative absorptions (*samādhis*). Mastery over them is the power of control (*vaśitva*) for entering and emerging from those states. *Vidyā* is the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). *Indrajāla* is the creation and display of armies and so forth, as well as their disappearance, according to the circumstances, whether they exist or do not exist. *Mohana* is the production of fainting. *Stambhana* is the rendering motionless. *Māraṇa* is the killing of those who cause extreme harm to the Three Jewels and so forth. *Uccāṭana* is the expulsion from one's place. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [is meant] the breaking of limbs, fever, possession by spirits (*graha*), possession by demons (*rākṣasa*), and so on. (13)

"Subjugated" (*vaśya*) means having come under control. Here, however, the ritual action for the purpose of subjugation is called "subjugation. There are two types of attraction: attraction by the feet and attraction by the body-mass (*piṇḍa*). The first is performed by means of the earth; the second, by means of space. These three actions are the rituals of subjugation and attraction. "Entering another city" refers to entering another body; this is expressed by the term *parapura*. By the word "etcetera," [powers such as] leaping over [distances] and so forth are included. Those very effects are the "effects of the other-city and so forth. "Invisibility" means the states of being unseen. (14)

*Vidveṣaṇa* (enmity) is the causing of mutual hatred even between those who are in love with one another. *Jambhana* is the act of silencing. *Pātālagamana* is the entry into a subterranean cavern (*bila*). A *mahāvidyādhara* is a sovereign (*cakravartin*) among the *vidyādharas*, one capable of both punishing and favoring them; his state is their true nature (*tattva*). "Freedom from old age," "immortality," and "freedom from disease"—these three are also easy to understand, and the meaning is implied by the word "and" (*ca*), namely, freedom from disease.

The remainder [of the meaning] is that all this, beginning with delusion (*mohana*), is performed by him who possesses the knowledge of *yogamāyā*. Regarding "illusion" (*māyā*): it is the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). Knowledge itself is "knowledge" (*vidyaḥ*). The "union" (*yoga*) is the single flavor of all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*). That which is both union and the knowledge of illusion is *yogamāyāvidya*.

The half-verse beginning with "Vidyādhara... consists of seventeen syllables; the verse beginning with "Nirvyādhī... consists of fourteen syllables. Among these, some applications for the rites of seizing all the qualities of a Buddha and so forth are to be explained in this very tantra, while others are to be understood according to other tantras.

It has been stated, "by mere consciousness"; the meaning is "by the mere performance [of the practice]. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that performance, he says "the imperishable," and so forth. "The imperishable" (akṣara) refers to the syllables of the mantra; "mantra-form" (mantrarūpa) refers to the embodiment born of the mantra. "The imperishable and the mantra-form"—the meaning is "by that [imperishable] and by those two [the imperishable and the mantra-form]. "They transform" (vikurvanti); they sport (vikrīḍanti) with the accomplishments (siddhis) of ritual action and so forth. "Yogins" refers to the practitioners (sādhakas). || 15-16 ||
He explains how one practices the syllable: "They recite" and "they contemplate. Here, recitation is chanting with speech; contemplation is chanting with the mind.

He explains how they practice the mantra-form with the words "visualizing" (*bhāvayanti*), and so forth. "Visualizing" means they see [the deity] through a continuous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "By means of meditative absorption" (*samādhinā*) means by means of the stability of the mind focused upon that [deity]. With the words "recited" (*paṭhitā*), and so forth, he states the fruit of the practice. "Recited" means muttered (*japtā*). "Vidyā" refers to Mahāmāyā. "She performs" means she performs all rites, such as summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) and others. By the second occurrence of the word "vidyā," the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) is expressed.

Furthermore, that perfection of the cultivation of the form is the clear vision of oneself in the aspect of one's own deity. It brings about accomplishment for the practitioner—that is, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. By the word "and" (ca), it also implies that one should accomplish ritual activities. The accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is the manifestation of oneself in the very form of one's own deity, visible both to oneself and to others. || 17 ||

He states the ease of practice [with the words] beginning with "not," etc. Here, the word "not" implies "one should cause [to be done]" (kārayet). The meaning is that one should not do it oneself. The rule (*niyama*) consists of bathing three times and changing clothes three times, and so forth.

Asceticism (*tapas*) consists of consuming food such as vegetables and barley-gruel. It is difficult to endure and painful. This is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) is fasting (*upavāsa*) and restraint (*saṃvara*). Among these, fasting is the abstention from food; restraint is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) even for a householder who possesses intense passion.

The "beneficial sensations" (*anugrāhikā vedanā*) are the pleasures (*sukha*) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses; those same [sensations] co-arising with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are the "joys" (*harṣa*). By means of these, practitioners achieve accomplishment.

The "Great Ḍākinī consisting of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī mahāḍākinī*) is either a woman externally who has been cultivated in that form as the Wisdom (*prajñā*), or the approach to her as the Means (*upāya*), which is the enjoyment by means of oneself cultivated in the form of Śrī Heruka.
From the word "etcetera," the five offerings and the five qualities of desire are included; "with these always" means at every junction of the day (*pratisandhya*). (18)

How, then, are they "joyful through wisdom and means"? To this he says: "The navel," and so forth. The "navel-lotus" is the navel; [the deity] is situated in its center. Who is he? He says: "The Hero. Because of his possession of unsurpassed heroism (*vīrya*), the Hero is Vajrasattva. In that regard, in what vessel does he reside? He says: "The pericarp," and so forth. "Having a hidden range" (*gūḍhagocara*) refers to one whose range is hidden within the pericarp of the navel-lotus. "Hidden" (*gūḍha*) means concealed or protected; "range" (*gocara*) means a vessel or receptacle for that purpose—thus, "having a hidden range."
The meaning is "the union of the sun and the moon. By this much, its locus and vessel have been described.

He states its intrinsic nature with the words beginning with "mind" (*citta*). "Mind" (*citta*) means consciousness (*vijñāna*). There are certain single-word expressions used for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); for example, one who eats only water is called "water-eater" (*abbhakṣa*), and one who eats only air is called "air-eater" (*vāyubhakṣa*). Likewise here as well, because there is no external object to be grasped apart from consciousness, the meaning of the word "mind" is that the universe is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).

That mind, too, is no-mind. Why? Because the mind lacks an object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Why is it no-mind? Because when there is no object of apprehension, there is also no subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*). For in the world, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is well known as that which apprehends objects; and here, "mind" (*citta*) is precisely this consciousness. Therefore, because it is both mind and no-mind, it is called "mind-no-mind" (*cittācitta*).

If that is "non-mind" (acitta) because it is devoid of the characteristic of mind consisting in the state of being a grasper, then by virtue of association with which characteristic of mind is it "mind"? To this he says: "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). Consciousness (*cit*) is sentience, the manifestation of awareness, luminosity, appearance, clarity, and—what amounts to the same thing—immediacy. That which has this as its form is "of the nature of consciousness. The meaning is that it is "mind" because of its association with the characteristic of mind consisting in the nature of consciousness.
[Objection: But all cognition (*vijñāna*) is of such a nature; what, then, is the distinction of the hero's own-being (*vīrasvabhāva*)? To this he says: "knowledge," and so forth.
"Sva" means one's own; "nijam rūpam" means intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

"Jñāna" and "jñeya" form a copulative compound (*dvandva*), resulting in "jñānajñeya. That which has this very intrinsic nature as its object of knowledge and knowledge is "jñānajñeyasvarūpaka. That by which something is known is "jñāna," and that which is known is "jñeya. In that regard, even for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the objects of their cognitions are not their [true] intrinsic nature, because they conceptualize a subject and an object even though neither exists, and because those two forms of subject and object—which are non-entities—appear within their cognitions. And that which does not exist, or which is not a real entity, cannot be the intrinsic nature of consciousness.

What then? It is superimposed by delusion (*bhrānti*). For this very reason, it is called the "cause of delusion," because it consists of a deluded mind. For those for whom the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) lacks its own intrinsic nature (*asvarūpa*), their cognition (*jñāna*) also lacks its own intrinsic nature; that is to say, it is delusion. For in this way, through the power of delusion, a non-existent thing or a non-entity appears. Therefore, that [delusion] is also a cognition, because it is the cause of that appearance. However, that delusion is not the innate form of the intellect (*buddhi*), because adventitious stains are extrinsic.

Therefore, their cognition is also not of the nature of [intrinsic] form. Ultimate bodhicitta, however, consists of non-conceptualizing knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*). "Conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*) is delusion. Since all conceptual proliferations are absent therein, its cognition is indeed its own intrinsic nature and not even delusion; because all causes of conceptual proliferation have set there and do not appear, its object of knowledge is its own intrinsic nature alone, and not even non-existent things.

Thus, by this half-verse, the nature of the hero (*vīra*) as the ultimate bodhicitta, characterized by the form of non-conceptual gnosis (*niḥprapañca-jñāna*), is directly stated; whereas its nature as great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is stated by implication, because great bliss is co-emergent with non-conceptual gnosis. As it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*: "Having become one whose intention is non-conceptual toward this True Dharma, O Son of the Conqueror, having transcended the difficult terrain of conceptualization, he gradually attains the state beyond conceptualization."
"Therefore, the bodhisattva attains that which is peaceful, immovable, supreme, self-controlled, peerless, and free from conceptual construction."

In these two verses, "non-conceptual intention" (*avikalpāśaya*) refers to a firm intention. "In this true Dharma" (*saddharme 'smin*) refers to the Mahāyāna. "Son of the Victor" (*jinātmaja*) refers to a bodhisattva. "Conceptualization itself" (*vikalpa eva*) is the fourfold difficult path; having gradually transcended—that is, passed beyond—it, one "attains the non-conceptual" (*niḥkalpam āpnuta*), meaning one attains non-conceptual, non-proliferated gnosis (*nirvikalpa-niḥprapañca-jñāna*). From that very gnosis, one attains non-conceptual bliss: it is "tranquil" because it is free from afflictions (*niḥkleśatvāt*); it is "immovable" because it is not subject to decline (*aparihāṇīyatvāt*).

It is supreme because it excels all worldly and supramundane happiness. It is sovereign because it can be manifested at will and for as long as one desires. It is equal because it is identical in its nature of happiness with other forms of happiness. It is unequal because of these very four distinctions. (19)

I shall speak of such a hero. To the question "In which vehicle is he renowned?", he says: "In the Buddha's teaching. That vehicle by which one becomes a Buddha is the Buddha's teaching; the meaning is the Mahāyāna.

[Objection: But has this not already been stated by the previous verse? Why, then, is it said, "I shall explain"? To this he replies: "Profound" (*gambhīra*). This means "in the profound Mahāyāna," that is to say, in the Mantra-yāna. For in the Mantra-naya, which is distinct from the Pāramitā-naya, the form of the *mudrā* and the equipment of the *bodhicitta* are cultivated as more swiftly accomplishing enlightenment; and that has not yet been spoken of. Therefore he says, "I shall explain."

He explains that very point with the words beginning "ālikālī" and so forth. "Therein" means within the union of the sun and moon. "Niyojitā" means employed for the sake of regulation. To the question "What [is it]? he says: "The line. That very line of rays has arisen from that same hero through the subtle aperture in the center of the moon; it is indivisible, uncuttable, and as fine as a lotus fiber. How is it employed? By making that very [line] equal to *āli* and *kālī*; that is, *āli* and *kālī* are made equal.

That [line] in which [they are] is so described. How are they in it? Because they are strung together in that very [line] by means of a pearl necklace (*muktāvalī*). How are they equal? Because two *kāli*s—referring to the half-*kāli*s—are denoted by the word *kāli*, since they are parts of a *kāli*; and those too consist of sixteen syllables due to the exclusion of *ṅ* and *ña*. Therefore, there is equality among them. And that line of rays encloses the *saṃpuṭa* with three coils. Upon that, a triple *āli* is strung above the moon, according to the recitation.
In the center there is the row of vowels (*svarālī*). These two have half-measures (*ardhakālī*). And so he will say: "divine, with rows of syllables.
And it is stated in the *Śrīsaṃvarottara*:
"One should arrange [the consonants] from *ka* to *da*, excluding *ṅa* and *ña*."

One should draw the two *ālīs* (vowel and consonant series) beginning with the letter *dha* and ending with the letter *kṣa*; the *ālī* of the letter *a*, situated in the middle, should be placed upon the lunar disc. || 20 ||

"Blazing," and so forth. When another streak of light, blazing with the fire of the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*), issues forth from the Hero, then it becomes that which causes downward flow. For here, the meaning of "flow" (*sruti*) is expressed by the word "flows" (*sravati*); thus, the sense is "flow. Now, he asks: what flows in that flow? He says: "Nectar" (*amṛta*). It is called nectar because it is liberation, because it is indestructible, and because it is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "having the form of a drop (*bindu*). This means that the Hero is white in color and has the nature of the drop of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). To the question "In what manner does it flow?", he says: "in the form of semen (*śukra*). Because the essence of pure gnosis (*viśuddhajñāna-rasa*) shares the common characteristics of semen by virtue of being a white, blissful fluid, it is designated by the word "semen.
It flows, or trickles, in that form; that is to say, it emits.

In this context, the excellence of the Hero (vīra) is described by the passage beginning with "alikālī"; his activity (*karma*) by the passage beginning with "jvalitā"; his alternative nature (*svabhāvāntara*) by the term "amṛta"; and his form as a seal (*mudrākāra*) by the phrase "in the form of a drop" (*bindurūpiṇam*). But how does this become his seal? It is said: that subtle drop, white as the moon, is the mind (*citta*), because it shines forth within.

Furthermore, that which is the mind’s abiding in that alone is "mind-only" (*cittamātratā*) because of the non-perception of any object external to the mind. That which is its state of being a non-grasper due to the absence of a graspable object is its "non-mindness" (*acittatā*). For this very reason, it has the nature of emptiness (*śūnyarūpa*). Moreover, that which is its luminosity is its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*). Furthermore, the subsiding of all signs of conceptual proliferation for the mind established in that alone is its nature as both knowledge and the object of knowledge (*jñānajñeyarūpatā*). And this is the form of the subtle wisdom-seal (*sūkṣmajñānamudrā*) of this Vajradhara. It is also stated in the *Śrīsamāja*:
One should meditate on a moon mandala situated in the center of the space element;
having visualized the form of the Buddha, one should commence the subtle yoga.
One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose, and within that mustard seed, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

"One should meditate upon the delightful state of gnosis, the secret fashioned by gnosis. This subtle yoga of his, along with its ritual application, is also described in the *Śrīvajrāmṛta* as common [to all]:
"While the Vidyā remains motionless, one should begin the meditation on nectar (*amṛta*)."
One meditates upon the supreme reality, the nectar in the form of a drop;
it is described as the reality of emptiness, resembling the moon in the center of space,
imperishable, undecaying, subtle, the unstruck Vajrasattva.
"The God, situated in the center of the navel within the hidden sphere of the pericarp,
flows in the form of semen, residing between the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*.
Therefore, exactly as it is recited, such is the yoga and the ritual action here."
However, in this tantra, one should not meditate on four wheels in the four locations, nor on Caṇḍālī.

It is not the case that, by her blazing, she heats the four wheels, emerges, and radiates forth, heating the four wheels of all the Buddhas, then returns, enters the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), and causes the flow of nectar from the syllable *Haṃ*.

Furthermore, whatever has been seen elsewhere is brought here by some; that is incorrect, because there is no authoritative statement [to that effect] and because all tantras have various intentions, whereas this tantra is of a very concise nature of realization (*abhisamaya*). (21)

With the words "Whatever... and so forth, he describes another ritual action. The sense faculties—the eye and the others—should take on, or attain, the state of being the path, that is, the state of being the object. Whatever object whatsoever is seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched, one should determine each and every one of those to consist of all Buddhas, having the nature of all Buddhas without exception.

How is it "consisting of all Buddhas"? By way of its own nature—that is to say, by its very essence or primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For thus the *dharmadhātu*, which is without beginning or end, is the primordial nature of all phenomena (*dharma*). And that very *dharmadhātu* is the supreme form of all Buddhas. Therefore, by virtue of that nature, each of those [deities] consists of all Buddhas. It is not only by way of its own nature, but also through the yoga of supreme placement (*paramāhitayoga*). Even without that [yoga], because the meaning is understood, it is called "supreme."

Supramundane gnosis is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and is called "the Hero" (*vīra*); that by which the means are established—that is, produced—is the "supreme benefit," meaning it is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Hero. "Yoga" with respect to that is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). By means of this conviction, whatever appears in vision and so forth—such as the visible object and so on—is the very natural outflow of the Hero; such is the meaning of "by this conviction. (22)

With the words "The great pledge" (*mahāsamaya*) and so forth, he describes another ritual action. "Pledge" (*samaya*) refers to the deity. The "great pledge" (*mahāsamaya*) is the lord of the mandala together with the mandala. Its "attainment" (*siddhi*) is its accomplishment. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of filling the meter. That attainment is the practice of the great pill (*mahāgulikā*). The pill is the drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*); the central drop, surrounded by four drops, is the great pill. The practice is the production [of that state] by means of it; it is the attainment of the great pledge.

He explains what one should do once the maṇḍala has been accomplished, beginning with the words "Mahāmāyā" and so forth. Mahāmāyā is the Lord of the Maṇḍala, Śrī Heruka; his consort, Buddhadākinī, is also Mahāmāyā, because the two possess a single nature. Through their applications—that is, their ritual actions such as embracing, kissing, and so on—one should cause [the disciple] to undertake the *yogasaṃvara*. Both "yoga" and "saṃvara" constitute *yogasaṃvara*. In this context, "yoga" refers to a subtle white drop within the interior of the union of the sun and moon at the pericarp of the navel-lotus.

That which was previously stated by the verse beginning with "the action blazes" (*karma jvalitā*) and so forth, concerning the restraint (*saṃvara*), the excellent bliss, and the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) following the investigation of penetration (*prativedha-vicāraṇā*). || 23 ||

Is it only this? No, he says: "five," and so forth. The meaning is that it is accompanied by these ten. Precisely from that semen of gnosis (*jñānaretas*) which has entered the interior of the *ḍākinī*’s lotus, there occurs the sequential manifestation of ten clouds of flowers and so forth, each pervading space.
They are called "offerings" (*upahāra*) because they are presented; [they are] flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and food offerings.

Those not yet attained are desired and longed for, thus they are called *kāma* (desires). Those already attained are multiplied and enjoyed again and again, thus they are called *guṇa* (qualities). Being both desires and qualities, they are *kāmaguṇa* (objects of sensual desire). These are the excellent forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects. In that regard, the restraint [of these] constitutes secret worship and the worship of reality (*tattva*). The remaining [offerings] constitute external worship.

Regarding this propitiation of the deity, he states the result with the words beginning "is to be known" (*jñātavyam*). It is to be known and determined. Because it is indeclinable (*avyaya*), it is ultimate; because it is imperishable, it is eternal—the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*). The ellipsis is "I shall attain that. (24)

Having thus briefly explained cultivation along with its benefits, he now describes the recitation (*jāpa*) together with the benefits common to all forms of cultivation, beginning with the words "By which... and so forth. "By knowledge" means by the *vidyā*. "By the perfected" means by that which has been practiced. "The abode of the thirty" refers to the realm of the gods (*devas*). "O Goddess" is an address to Buddha-Ḍākinī.
To the question, "Is this true or not? he replies, "It is true," and so forth. An emphatic restriction is understood: the meaning is that I speak only the truth and never a falsehood. (25)

Then, [the question arises]: "What deity is that gnosis? What is its power? And what is its nature? To this, he says: "That I... and so forth. Because of the connection with the words "I shall speak" (*vakṣyāmi*) in relation to the accusative case in "you" (*tvām*) and so on, the answer to "What deity? is: "You, the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), the Vidyā. The answer to "What is its power? is: "The accomplisher of the three worlds (*trailokyasādhanī*). The answer to "What is its nature? is: "The divine of the Great Yoginīs (*mahāyoginīdivyam*). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). It is "divine" (*divya*) because they sport (*dīvyanti*) within it; the meaning is the secret union of the Sun and Moon.

For that is their state of equality; therefore, that alone is the locus of delight for yogins. "By lines of syllables" means it is adorned by three lines consisting of vowels and consonants—this is the remainder [of the sense]. The hero situated in the center is Śrī Heruka; he is the "union" (saṃpuṭa), meaning the Buddha-Ḍākinī. || 26 ||

"By which" means by that which is presided over by the Hero, namely the union of the sun and moon, adorned with the three rows of vowels and consonants. "Merely by being thought of" means merely by being recited. How the recitation is to be performed, he will explain in the second instruction. "The moving and the unmoving" refers to the external triple world. "Is accomplished" means it becomes subject to one's control. "The yogi who is served" means by whom? By the Vajrayoginīs. "According to their wish" means in whatever manner they desire. "They show" means they grant a vision to him. "The self of yoga" refers to the deities of the mantra. (27–28)

"He gives" means he bestows. "Great accomplishment" refers to the eightfold [siddhis], such as the sword, collyrium, and so forth. "Tāthāgatī" (belonging to the Tathāgatas): because they have realized suchness (*tathatā*), they are Tathāgatas—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this is their *tāthāgatī* glory, that is, their excellence. "Perform" means that very same yogi. (29)

"Intoxicant" (*madya*) means the extraction of intoxicants. "Having drawn" (*āhṛtya*) means having extracted. "Life-force" (*āyuḥ*) is vitality; "vigor" (*vīrya*) is enthusiasm; "splendor" (*tejaḥ*) is power; and "divine eye" (*divyaṃ cakṣuḥ*) is visual consciousness.
"And supernatural power" (*ṛddhim*) refers to the superknowledge of miraculous powers (*ṛddhyabhijñā*).
"Soma-drinking" (*somapānam*) is the drinking of nectar (*amṛta*). "Day by day" (*dine dine*) means every single day. "He obtains"—this completes the verse. (30–31)

"Long-lived" has been mentioned; its detailed explanation begins with "he," and so forth. That yogi would go to—that is, attain—an extensive and vast lifespan. It is described as such because a great eon (*mahākalpa*) constitutes its limit and conclusion.

He is called a *yogin* because he demonstrates [these powers]. That by which sentient beings are drawn toward and converted is a *pratihārya*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), thus it becomes *prātihārya*. And that is threefold: the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), and the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*). These correspond respectively to the three superknowledges (*abhijñā*): the power of supernormal success (*ṛddhi*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*). "A body of unsurpassed beauty" refers to a physical form that never tires the sight; this connects with the preceding verb "he demonstrates. (32)

One’s own nature (*svarūpa*) is one’s essential form; its transformation is the assumption of another form. "Mentally conceived" means merely a mental murmuring (*manojalpa*), such as the thought, "May I become of such a form. Concluding by way of praise, he says: "The Vidyā," and so forth.

In the expression "accomplished through recitation" (*paṭhitasiddhā*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the present tense. The meaning is that it is accomplished by mere recitation (*jāpamātreṇa*). It is called "Infallible" (*Amoghinī*) because of its connection with infallible power; for when it is accomplished, it necessarily bestows the results as described. || 33 ||

"O Vidyā! There is no other knowledge equal to you, similar to you, for me, in the three worlds"—that is, within the three families of the Tathāgata, Vajra, and Padma. "Āgama" means the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). "O Beautiful One! is an address of invocation. (34)
As the aspect of skillful means, she is the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśvarī); as the aspect of wisdom (prajñā), she is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā). And who is she? She is Mahāmāyā.
Her accomplishment is her practice; its cause is its sign. Its various powers are their exposition—that is, their description.
The first chapter in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Śrīmahāmāyā*. || 1 ||

Now, regarding the passage beginning with *athāta* and so forth: this is a twelve-syllable verse consisting of a single line. The word *atha* (now) serves to introduce the entire recitation (*japa*). The word *ataḥ* (from this) means after the meditation on the form of the deity. "Divine" refers to the *savīra* (with-hero) vessel of the Great Yoginīs; the ellipsis to be supplied is that one should contemplate [it] within the pericarp of the navel-lotus. To the question of what is to be recited therein, he says: *guhya* and so forth. It is "secret" (*guhya*) because it is not to be disclosed, or else it is secret because by means of it the reality (*tattva*) of the deity is concealed.

It is both secret and imperishable. Yoga is the meditative absorption (samādhi) on the deity. Its accomplishment (siddhi) is its completion; the fruit of that very completion is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā). Because it bestows those two preeminently, it is called "the bestower of the fruit of the accomplishment of yoga. || 1 ||

"By mere thought" means even without the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), by mere recitation (*japa*). The "desired boon," such as the state of a *vidyādhara* and so forth, is attained. The intended meaning is that one should see the secret syllable within the interior of the *sampuṭa*, raise the Hero (*vīra*) above it, and then recite.

To the question "How should one recite?", he says: "The first," and so forth. Here, the "first syllable" is the *praṇava* (Oṃ), because it is generally seen at the beginning of mantras. "By its application" means by its slow pronunciation. The connection is: "the yogi performs. What does he perform? Exhalation—the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). || 2 ||

"By the end of the eighth" means by the letter *ha*, which is the final member of the eighth group; this is the connection [to the verb]. How does one perform it? It is joined with the vowel *ū* beneath the *ha*, and with the nasal bindu upon the head of the *ha*; such is the collective meaning of the syllable *hūṃ*. He asks:

what kind of exhalation and inhalation does one perform? He replies: "devoid of existence and non-existence. The words "in due order" are to be understood as the ellipsis. For the meaning of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is pure gnosis (*jñānamātratā*), according to the statement in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*: "The syllable Oṃ is the heart of gnosis."

The meaning of the syllable *hūṃ* is the equality of body, speech, and mind by virtue of being without appearance (*nirābhāsa*). For it is said in that very same source: "The syllable *hūṃ* brings about the indivisibility of the three vajras—body, speech, and mind.

Therefore, because one perceives the universe indicated by the syllable *oṃ* as being nothing but mind (*cittamātratā*), it is "devoid of existence" (*bhāvavarjita*). That very universe, which is nothing but mind, is non-existence (*abhāva*), for there is no existence of entities apart from the mind. The attainment of the equality of that universe—which is nothing but mind—and its becoming free from appearance is what is indicated by the syllable *hūṃ*. Because of perceiving that, it is "devoid of non-existence" (*abhāvavarjita*). Thus, it is devoid of both existence and non-existence.

In that case, what is the nature of the vision of the state of being mere-cognition (*cittamātratā*) and the attainment of equality? Here is the instruction: While pronouncing the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), one should visualize a line of rays of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*) emerging from the Hero (*vīra*) along with the exhalation. Having pervaded [all things] with it, there is the transformation of the universe into the nature of the Buddha. "While pronouncing the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), the visualization of that universe in the form of one's own deity" is the vision of the state of being mere-mind.

Then, by means of the exhalation of the syllable *hūṃ*, there is the withdrawal of the universe into the Hero (*vīra*) and the vision of the attainment of equality. One should perform both of these slowly and repeatedly as long as no fatigue arises; this is the recitation (*jāpa*) in this tantra. (3)

Here, he describes the ease of practice with the words beginning "na tasya" (not for him). "Tasya" refers to one who is reciting. "Vrata" refers to the observances such as silence, bathing, and begging for alms. "Yantraṇā" and "dhāraṇā" refer to the restraint and retention of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). "Nivartante" means they do not follow from other systems (*tantrāntara*). The sense of "one after another" (*aparāparam*) is also understood; the meaning is that all other external rituals besides these also cease. || 4 ||

Now, is recitation (*japa*) merely verbal muttering? In this context, should one perform only the verbal muttering, or should there also be the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the form and the gnosis? To this, he says: "The mantra... and so forth. Yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has reality as its object. That yoga is threefold, of three types. Why? Because it consists of mantra, form, and dharma. A mantra is speech that illuminates reality. The form is the body of the deity. Dharma is the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra.

"By means of the threefold knowledge" refers to the three yogas just mentioned, and not by mere verbal discourse. "Is not defiled by the faults of existence" means that one is liberated from the defects of saṃsāra, such as evil deeds and so forth. || 5 ||

"Thus" refers to the three yogas. "Constantly" means every day. "Perpetually" means at each junction of the day (sandhyā). "Is accomplished" means it is perfected. "Vajrasattva" is Śrī Heruka; "equal to him" means similar to him. By the word "also," [it implies] equal to Vajraḍākinī. "He" refers to the yogin. Therefore, in this context, the form of Heruka and the ḍākinīs should be meditated upon with the sense of identity (*tad-ahaṃkāra*).

The *mantras* are the *praṇava* and the syllable *hūṃ*, being uttered slowly; and in their midst, the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) is also to be uttered slowly. Regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra: one should understand that by raising the *vīrabindu* upon the head of the syllables of the *vidyā* situated within the cavity formed by the union of the Sun and Moon, and by means of the ray emitted from it, all phenomena are rendered as consisting of the Buddha and then reabsorbed into the *vīrabindu*.

Thus, when the recitation has been performed for six months through the application of the mantra, its form, and its dharma, whether or not a corresponding accomplishment (siddhi) has been attained, the syllables of the vidyā, when correctly employed, necessarily accomplish their respective rites.

In order to indicate the syllables of the *vidyā* and their applications, he says "Indravarṇa," and so forth. By the word "Indra," the *indrāgopa* (the cochineal insect) is meant. The first syllable is the *praṇava* (oṃ). One should perform the meditation on that [syllable] for the sake of attracting whomsoever one intends. "Vidyā" refers to the practitioner of the *vidyā* (*vidyā-yogī*). That yogi quickly brings that person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) under his power. The indication of "quickly" is "in an instant" (*kṣaṇāt*). This is what is meant:

Having performed the yoga of the Buddha-Ḍākinī and others, which is reddish like saffron, one should contemplate the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) as reddish like saffron within the vessel of the hero (*vīra*). Having placed the hero within its drop (*bindu*), one should turn the hero red with the rays of the *praṇava*. Then, having caused two lines of reddish rays to issue forth from the hero—one should contemplate a noose at the tip of one and a hook at the tip of the second. Having bound the object of practice (*sādhya*) by the throat with the noose and pierced him in the heart with the hook, one should contemplate him being swiftly drawn forth. In a mere moment, he becomes drawn forth. || 7 ||

"Second," and so forth. In the *āli* reading, the second syllable is the letter *ā*. [The hero] is joined with that; he raises up its head. By means of that, the practitioners of the yoga of one's own deity meditate and color [the object] down to the level of atoms.
"Vibhāvana" means the cultivation of various things to be accomplished (*sādhyabhāvana*).
"All those" refers to the totality of the factors to be accomplished, and so forth. The sense of "even" (*api*) is understood;
the meaning is that he brings even the entire three worlds under his control, let alone a hundred or a thousand living beings.

What is meant [by this]? Having made the union of any one of the six [syllables] red as the *javā* flower, and having placed the letter *Ā*—red as the *javā*—within the hollow of the hands (*saṃpuṭa*), one should place the Hero (*vīra*) upon its head, colored by that very [letter]. One should then contemplate that, by means of its rays, the atoms of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) are colored, and that they have been brought under control and fallen at one's feet; thus, all of them come under one's power. || 8 ||

"Brahmā," and so forth. Kāmeśvara is Māra. These [beings], Brahmā and the others, are drawn forth. Because it is imperishable (*akṣaya*), "syllable" (*akṣara*) refers to the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*). Its secret syllable is the "syllable of syllables" (*akṣarākṣara*). In some recensions, the reading is *akṣarajñāna*; in that case, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the seed-syllable, meaning the *HŪṂ* residing in both. And that [syllable] is deep-red like the *javā* flower during the act of drawing forth. Being impelled—that is, urged—by that. How are they impelled? Like the initial practice of drawing forth. Others say that the drawing forth here occurs by means of the exhalation of the *HŪṂ* syllable.
In this tantra, some say that all the applications for summoning are performed by means of the trunks of the rays arising from the Hero. (9)

He speaks of the supreme summoning of the *piṇḍa* with the words beginning "with the form" (*ākāra*) and so forth. "Endowed with those two" means practitioners who are properly endowed with both the form and the syllable—that is, with either the form or the syllable *hūṃ*.
"The threefold conjunction" (*trisaṃyoga*) refers to the union of the three. "Situated in body, speech, and mind" means abiding in the body, throat, and heart of the object to be accomplished.

What is meant [by this]? Having colored one of the six [syllables] with the hue of *javā*, and having placed the Hero upon the head of the letter *Ā* or within the dot (*bindu*) of the syllable *HŪṂ* inside the *saṃpuṭa*, one should visualize the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) mounted upon a wind-mandala arising from the syllable *YAṂ*. With two lines of rays red as *javā* emanating from the Hero, one should imagine him bound by a noose and pierced in the heart respectively by a hook at his throat, and then swiftly drawn through the atmosphere. In an instant, he is summoned. || 10 ||

"Khekāra," and so forth. This is what is meant: having visualized oneself as white, four-faced, with a skull and noose in hand, and with a red mind by means of the syllable *khe*, one should contemplate that the semen of the target is drawn out by a tube of light rays arising from the hero situated at the head of the syllable *khe* and entering the secret place of the target; one should think that it is being placed within the skull. In an instant, it is drawn forth. || 11 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "the syllable *ci*": having visualized oneself as Hayagrīva, yellow in color and yellow in radiance, by means of the short syllable *ci*, one should imagine drawing up the liquor contained in the vessel with the trunk-like ray of the Hero situated upon the head of the syllable *ci*, thereby filling the container; it becomes filled in an instant. || 12 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "rakāre" and so forth: having visualized oneself as red-colored, four-armed, four-faced, with the face of a jackal, and possessing great luster, yet wrathful—by means of a leech-like ray of light, one should contemplate, as before, blood being drawn from the body of the target. (13–14ab)

In the applications of one's own deity (*svadevatāyoga*), this six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) consists of these very syllables of the *vidyā*. Therefore, following the context, he explains that as well with the words beginning "six," and so forth. The connection is as follows: one should contemplate [the deity] as being joined with those six syllables of the *vidyā*—that is, the six phonemes just mentioned. The phrase "the body of one's own deity" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

To the question "Where is it joined?", he says: "In six locations. This means in six places. This being so, the Vajrayoginīs are accomplished, and not otherwise. "Vajra" refers to Heruka; "Yoginīs" refers to the five Ḍākinīs. "Yoga" refers to Śrī Heruka. When there is the supreme bliss with those very Yoginīs in the *Ḍākinīsaṃvara* of that [Heruka], it is said to be "in six locations. He states those very locations with the words beginning with "eye," etc.; "mind" refers to the heart; and by the word "and" (*ca*), the tongue and the body are included. (14cd–15)

He states another yoga, beginning with “siṃha” and so forth. It is so called because it is that in which there is the playful sport (*vikrīḍita*) of the Lion, who is the Hero (*vīra*). Regarding “the mudrā”: it is the union (*sampuṭa*) of the sun and moon. “Binding” means they visualize her as bound, by means of three lines of syllables as before. Regarding “the yogins”: they are established in the yoga of Śrī Heruka surrounded by the four goddesses. Regarding “breath control” (*prāṇāyāma*): it refers to inhalation and exhalation. Regarding “well-restrained”: the meaning is having well restrained them by making them subtle in sequence. “Having meditated” means...
Having fixed the mind right there in the Hero, visible through the opening of the moon-like aperture, it blazes up at that very moment. || 16 ||
For one whose mind is stabilized in the heroic state, knowledge blazes forth instantly; it brings about illumination.

He states how far it blazes: "in the seven worlds" (*saptaloka*). The seven worlds are the netherworld (*pātāla*), the earth (*bhūḥ*), heaven (*svargaḥ*), and the first, second, third, and fourth meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). The collective totality of these is "the seven worlds," which is neuter like the term "the three worlds" (*tribhuvana*). Each of the [first] three meditative absorptions consists of three levels, while the fourth consists of eight levels. Its eighth level is Akaniṣṭha. Therefore he says: "up to the world of Akaniṣṭha. Therein, the mobile beings are the sentient beings; the immobile are the celestial palaces, abodes, and so forth. Therefore he says: "with the mobile and the immobile" (*sacarācara*).

Now, in order to demonstrate both the visibility and invisibility of that hero to all sentient beings, he says: "They cultivate," and so forth. "All" refers to all sentient beings. "Cultivate" means they practice repeatedly, because they perceive their own minds in various ways. And yet, "they do not understand him" because they do not see reality (*tattva*); for he appears to the foolish only through unreal forms. (17)

"The play of the world" (*jagatkrīḍā*) means the play of the universe; it is the conceptualization of duality through various forms. [If one were to say] "it perishes," it would have already perished previously; yet even now it has not perished. Because it is thus, therefore: "this knowledge" refers to the reality of knowledge (*jñānatattva*), which is non-dual and called "Vīra. "Hidden" means concealed from the ignorant. By what? By delusions that display unreal forms. Of what nature is it? It is unmanifest because it is beyond the range of speech; it is without syllables because it is not an object of mental chatter. (18)

To the question, "Who then perceives this in the ultimate sense? he says: "Those who understand," and so forth. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used for emphasis and is displaced in its position [in the sentence]. "The Fully Awakened Ones" (*saṃbuddhāḥ*) means precisely the Tathāgatas. If the perception of that [reality] by the Tathāgatas were established by their very nature (*prakṛtisiddha*), then others would certainly have no access to it. If, on the other hand, it were dependent upon yoga, then others too might perceive it through that very same yoga; therefore, he says "by yoga," and so forth.

Because of its state of absolute non-distraction, it resembles sleep; thus, "sleep" (*nidrā*) is like actual sleep. This is "yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*). Having become united with, or joined to, that [sleep], they are described by the words "meditating," and so forth. "Forms" (*rūpāṇi*) refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). "Single" (*eka*) means having the single flavor of mere luminosity devoid of appearances (*nirābhāsaprakāśamātraikarasa*).

"Piṇḍa" means that very [object], which, because it is completely condensed and rendered extremely subtle, is a "piṇḍa"—that is to say, a mere drop as subtle as a mustard seed. By this, the form of the Hero's mudrā is established. "With minds fixed upon that" means having their consciousness abiding in that very piṇḍa. By this, the meaning of yogic sleep (yoganidrā) is indicated. || 19 ||

He states the *samaya*—the cause for the accomplishment of such yogas—with the words beginning "bhāvayanti" (they should meditate). "Bhāvayanti" means one should have resolute conviction (*adhimucyet*). What should one have resolute conviction in? Those objects that arise from the nine gates. Of what nature should one have resolute conviction? That they are of the nature of the Buddhas; that is to say, they are of the essence of Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Lokeśa, and Amoghasiddhi, who are eternal. One should consume those very objects for the purpose of consuming conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). "By the non-conceptual" means without hesitation. "By the absence of intrinsic nature" means...
"By means of the non-appearance of the grasped and the grasper"—the remainder [of the sentence] is: "by the mind of the wise one," which culminates in mere luminosity. || 20 ||

"Regarding 'the thumb,' and so forth: [at] the gate is the Cintāmaṇi. The meaning is that the Cintāmaṇi is situated at the tips of the thumb and the ring finger. The sense is that one should then consume those very [substances] by means of that [finger-gesture]. When? He says: "When the nectar," and so forth. This means when all of that has been transformed into the nature of nectar according to the procedure to be described. What will happen then? He says: "Accomplishment," and so forth. (21)

The term *yogeśvarī mahāvidyā* has been explained. Her "yoga" is the union of the *bindu* within the enclosure of the sun and moon. The manner in which that [union] is described by means of the passage beginning with "the lion’s play" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) constitutes its determination (*nirṇaya*). Its "instruction" (*nirdeśa*) is the exposition thereof.
The second instruction in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyā*. || 2 ||

"Others" means those different from the nine just mentioned. "Substance-groups" (dravyagaṇas) refers to those which are both substances and groups, because each one constitutes a portion of a group. "O Omniscient One" means those who bestow the fruit that is omniscience itself. (1)
"By which" means by which collection of substances. "The Mothers of the Elements" refers to the Vajra-Ḍākinīs. (2)

Endowed with greatness is the "great palala. The word *tathā* is used in the sense of conjunction. Regarding the phrase "on the fourteenth," and so forth: here, the short vowel for the eighth day and the long vowel for Jambūka are archaic (chāndasa) forms. The term *asaha* applies to each [ingredient]. "Having meditated upon" means having smeared and dried them with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) over seven days. (3–4)

"Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight"—having done this, and subsequently "having joined them together," meaning having unified them, they are to be placed within the body of Śiva during the night of the spirits (*bhūtarātri*). These are the things to be placed. As for "those": the substances thus consecrated and established are *siddhārtha* fruits, that is, [seeds] the size of mustard seeds. (5)

What, then, are those substances? He says: "five. This means five *palas*. Likewise, regarding the measure: because it is an illustration, such a configuration is also [implied]. It is said "in this tantra" in its entirety. For this very reason he says: "and in other tantras," and so forth. "Not everything has been stated" means that not all has been spoken. To the question "what follows from that?", he says: "it is concealed. Having done what is it concealed? He says: "having understood them to be of great fruit."

The meaning is: "having known those [five] to be of great fruit. Why are they of great fruit? Because the five aggregates—when cultivated through the five gnoses, established in the limb of peace (*śivāṅga*), and situated within the *sampuṭa* vessel—attain identity with the Hero (*vīrasārūpyagamana*). || 6 ||

"Then," and so forth. "Then" means immediately following. The meaning is that whatever practice (*sādhana*) is contained in this tantra—by which ritual action the Blessed One together with his maṇḍala is accomplished and propitiated—that is presented here.

"One should visualize a lotus": having made the world equal to space through the meditation on the non-manifest bodhicitta, and having contemplated the ground as consisting of vajras, one should contemplate an eight-petaled or four-petaled lotus within a peaked pavilion situated in the midst of the eight terrifying cremation grounds.
"Of uniform red color" means both red and possessing a red luster.

"By means of the mind" (*manasā*) means that it is characterized by the drop of the perfectly pure *manovindu* known as "Hero" (*vīra*), which, while residing in the pericarp, radiates forth and remains situated upon the petals in the four directions.

"Accompanied by the four goddesses" means that when there is a radiation from each of the drops on the eastern petals and so forth of the Vajra, Maṇi, Padma, and Karma families, as well as of their respective infinite lineages (*kula*), [the deity] is seated upon those very petals by the Vajra, Ratna, Padma, and Viśva-Ḍākinīs produced through the process of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*). || 7 ||

"Adorned by the image of the Buddha": the Buddha is Vajradhara; his image (bimba) is his form, Śrī Heruka. It is adorned by him, the leader of the maṇḍala. Through those very goddesses, from the root mental bindu—which has been impelled by the songs to be described and has transformed into the form of the two seed-syllables—the directions are pervaded by the radiation of the lords of the five families and their respective families. Then, through the withdrawal of that [radiation], by means of the transformation of the central bindu and the two seed-syllables that have emerged, there arises the yoga with the Blessed One Śrī Heruka, who is embraced by Buddhadākinī.
Furthermore, as to what that Buddha-image is like, he says: "In the east," and so forth. "Four-faced" means having four heads. "Four-armed and three-eyed" is easy to understand.

He states what the color is for each face: the eastern face is the color of a blue lotus; the southern face is yellow; the western face is white; and the northern face is red—this is the meaning. Furthermore, it is well known that whatever is the color of the primary face, that is the very same color of the body. "Filled with garlands of flames" means that he is crowded with garlands of flames equal to the fire of universal destruction (pralaya-anala). || 8–9 ||

With the words beginning with "on the left" (vāme), he describes the emblems of the goddesses. "She who has a khaṭvāṅga and a bell on the left" means *vāmakhaṭvāṅgaghaṇṭā*. "Likewise, she who holds a vajra and a skull-cup in her right hands" means she who has a vajra and a skull-cup in her two hands; thus she is so described. "In the east" means on the eastern petal. "The goddess" (*devīm*)—this term is to be connected everywhere in what follows as well. Here, for now, it refers to Vajraḍākinī; subsequently, in due order, to Ratnaḍākinī, Padmaḍākinī, and Viśvaḍākinī. "On the right," and so forth.
She is so described because she holds in her hands a trident, a jewel, a banner, and a jackal.

The word "paścimena" (with the west) is used in the sense of the locative case. She is the "bearer of the bow, arrow, universal lotus, and skull" (*dhanurbāṇaviśvapadmakapālinī*) by virtue of possessing these. Regarding the phrase beginning with "khaḍga": she is so described because she holds in her hands a sword, a noose, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and a skull. These [deities] are also surrounded by garlands of flames, have four faces, four arms, and three eyes, because qualities follow the nature of the principal [deity].

Therefore, following the sequence of the faces of the Blessed One, the eastern face is blue, the southern yellow, the western white, and the northern dark green. Their faces are likewise; however, their root face has the color of their body. In place of the body-colored face of the Blessed One, they have a blue face. 10.

He describes the signs of the Blessed One’s station with the words beginning with “body” (*kāya*). Śrī Heruka is the vajra of body, speech, and mind; one should contemplate him there—in the red lotus—specifically in the center, that is, upon the pericarp. Regarding the phrase “the skull-cup,” etc., the remainder [of the sentence] is “in his hands. Just as Śrī Heruka is, so too is Buddhāḍākinī; however, she is red in color and has a red primary face. She faces him, her neck firmly embraced by his two arms. (11)

Since there is no accomplishment without the *samaya*, he speaks in order to explain the "ignition of the *samaya*," beginning with the words "At first" (*ādau*) and so forth. The "initial mantra" (*ādimantra*) is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). The connection is that the *samaya*-substance, when conjoined with that, blazes. Regarding the word "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*): it means when one has meditated according to the oral instruction. "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to the *samaya*-substance. "Accomplishes" (*sādhayate*) means he brings it to completion. What kind does he bring to completion? One that bestows the fruit of accomplishment (*siddhi*). And it is said in the glorious *Guhyasamāja*:
"Having meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* of all mantras, it blazes up at that very moment. (12)
He speaks of the benefits of kindling [the fire] with the words beginning "By yoga," and so forth.

Here, the term *yoga* refers specifically to the practitioners (*yogins*). The meaning is that people develop the conviction that there exist accomplished practitioners, both male (*yogin*) and female (*yoginī*), because they witness the display of power through the kindling of the fire. He describes the power resulting from the accomplishment of invisibility and other such feats with the words beginning "Invisible," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "illuminating a single thousandfold world": a *sāhasra-lokadhātu* is a world-system consisting of a thousand four-continent world-systems; he is the illuminator of one such [thousandfold] world-system by virtue of his sovereignty and his performance of the welfare of others. (13)

"Of all the siddhas" refers to those such as the vidyādharas; "a maiden" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The "vajra-abode" is the buddha-field established for those very buddhas; this assembly belongs to them. "Together with those two" means together with those established in the vajra-abode. (14)

“Eye-vajra” means the vajra-eye; the meaning is the superknowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*). “In his own hand,” and so forth, means as if there were a single *āmalaka* fruit situated in his own hand. “The fields” means the Buddha-fields and the sentient beings residing therein. “Characterized by body, speech, and mind” means: bodies and minds are the sensory consciousnesses (*indriya-jñāna*), while speech and minds are the mental consciousnesses (*mano-vijñāna*) because they involve discursive thought (*sajalpatva*). They “cultivate their characteristics” means they perceive them with the mind. How do they perceive them? The meaning is: “with one’s entire self, as one’s entire self.”
To the question "What is this?", he says: "Mind," and so forth. "Called mind" means the vajra-mind; the meaning is the superknowledge (*abhijñā*) of knowing the minds of others.

The cultivation of oneself in the form of one's own deity—in Yoga Tantra—that is here the "drama" (*nāṭaka*), because of its similarity to a drama. It is described as such because it arises from that.
In the accomplishment of the *samaya* substances, only a little has been said.

Since such auspiciousness exists even for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he distinguishes [the Buddha’s state] from them by saying "Reality" (*tattva*), which means the gnosis free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Bodhisattvas also possess such gnosis, but that is surpassed by the gnosis of a Buddha; therefore, for the sake of distinction, he says "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). It is "unsurpassed" because there is nothing superior to it. (15–16)
Regarding the phrase "here, the verse": this is a summary verse concerning the meaning of the tantra as it has been explained.

"Forms" refers to the colors and configurations of the deities and so forth. "Seals" (mudrās) refers to the acts of sealing, such as the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), the purification of the vajra and lotus, and so on. "Its very sign" refers to that same [sealing].

The skull-bowl, the khaṭvāṅga staff, and so forth; the substances are the articles of the *samaya*; "meditations" (*dhyāna*) means that *dhyai* signifies reflection, which is to say, recitations (*japa*); "cultivations" (*bhāvanā*) are the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the maṇḍala circle and so on; "various means" (*upāya*) are the ritual applications, the attainments of the lower accomplishments (*siddhi*), and so forth. All these have been demonstrated and indicated. To the question, "What has been accomplished by all this?", he says: "Of the Goddess," and so on. Whatever is desired by the mind, whatever is desired by the heart of the Goddess Mahāmāyā, those have been spoken. (17)

He states the benefits of embracing the *tantra* with the verse beginning with "the *tantra*," and so forth. "The *tantra*" refers to that which is called the *Mahāmāyā*. "In whose house" means in whose house it would always be; "always" means it should remain there constantly. "Should maintain" (*dhārayet*) means one should uphold it. "Should recite" (*vācayet*) means one should cause it to be recited; the meaning is that one should read it. "Should visualize" (*vibhāvayet*) means one should bring it to mind clearly. "Obstacles" (*vighnāni*) refers to hindrances. || 18 ||

And those who are great *vajraḍākinīs*—the doctrine (*mata*) of them, the philosophical system (*siddhānta*) embraced by them, is the entire *Yoginītantra*; this is the meaning. Its secret is its essence. What is that? He says: "The great secret. At the beginning it was called the "supreme secret," and at the end that very same thing is called the "great secret" by another synonym; the meaning is the tantra known as the *Mahāmāyā*. That is completed and finalized. "Along with the ritual services" (*sopacāram*).

The term *upacāra* refers to the method [of discourse] concerning the goal and the means of achievement (*sādhyasādhanārtha*). That which exists together with this is called *sopacāra*; the meaning is that it is not devoid of that.
Whatever merit has been acquired by me through composing this commentary on the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*, which possesses qualities like the luster of the full moon,
may it result in my becoming the singular self of the Victors, the state of the Vajra-holder.
"Then may the entire world attain the ultimate destruction of suffering.
Thus ends the third instruction in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyā*.
The Great Commentary on the Mahāmāyā, titled Guṇavatī, composed by the great paṇḍita Ratnākaraśānti, is hereby completed.
